stem: A 3-day-old boy becomes lethargic and starts vomiting. Ammonia is markedly raised with a normal anion gap, urine orotic acid is high and plasma citrulline is low. His mother's brother died in infancy.
oneliner: 3-day-old boy + vomiting, lethargy + high ammonia, normal anion gap + high urine orotic acid + low citrulline + maternal uncle died in infancy → where does the deficient enzyme work?
ask: In which subcellular compartment does the deficient enzyme normally work?

whyNot.A: Enzymes after citrulline work here; a defect there would **raise citrulline**, but his is **low**
whyNot.C: Handles drug and steroid metabolism, not the urea cycle steps that make **citrulline**
whyNot.D: Oxidizes very-long-chain fatty acids; it does not make **citrulline** from ornithine
whyNot.E: Holds acid hydrolases of storage diseases; its failure would not give **hyperammonemia with low citrulline**

why: **High ammonia, high orotic acid and low citrulline in a boy with an affected maternal uncle** indicate X-linked OTC deficiency. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and **OTC** both work in the **hepatocyte mitochondrial matrix**; citrulline then moves to the cytosol for the remaining steps.

idea.rule: The first two urea cycle enzymes (CPS I and OTC) are mitochondrial; the rest are cytosolic.
also: CPS I and OTC: mitochondrial matrix
Argininosuccinate synthetase and lyase, and arginase: cytosol
N-acetylglutamate synthase (activator of CPS I): mitochondrial matrix
OTC deficiency raises orotic acid; CPS I deficiency does not

stem: In an experiment on isolated muscle mitochondria, palmitate is oxidized only when carnitine is added, and malonyl-CoA blocks this oxidation. Oxidation of octanoate and of pyruvate is unaffected by carnitine or by malonyl-CoA.
oneliner: Isolated muscle mitochondria + palmitate oxidized only with carnitine + malonyl-CoA blocks it + octanoate and pyruvate unaffected → where is the inhibited enzyme?
ask: At which site does the carnitine-shuttle enzyme that malonyl-CoA inhibits sit?

whyNot.A: Site of **CPT-II**, which regenerates acyl-CoA in the matrix and is **not** the enzyme malonyl-CoA inhibits
whyNot.B: Where **malonyl-CoA** is made; the experiment uses **isolated mitochondria**, so the inhibited enzyme is part of the mitochondrion
whyNot.C: Handles very-long-chain fatty acids by a **carnitine-independent** route; the experiment concerns mitochondria
whyNot.E: An aqueous space that carries **acylcarnitine** but contains no malonyl-CoA-sensitive enzyme

why: Long-chain fatty acids need carnitine, while **octanoate and pyruvate enter freely**, so the block is the shuttle. **CPT-I** on the **outer mitochondrial membrane** converts acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine and is inhibited by **malonyl-CoA**; CPT-II on the inner membrane regenerates acyl-CoA in the matrix.

idea.rule: CPT-I (outer membrane, inhibited by malonyl-CoA) is the rate-limiting step of long-chain fatty acid oxidation.
also: CPT-II deficiency causes exertional rhabdomyolysis
Carnitine deficiency impairs long-chain fatty acid entry
Fed state: insulin raises malonyl-CoA and blocks CPT-I
Medium-chain fatty acids bypass the carnitine shuttle

stem: A healthy 25-year-old man has had nothing to eat for 12 hours overnight. His blood glucose is normal. He is not exercising, and his muscles are at rest.
oneliner: 25M + fasting 12 h overnight + normal blood glucose → which glycogen store keeps it up?
ask: Glycogen breakdown in which tissue is mainly keeping his blood glucose normal?

whyNot.A: Muscle lacks **glucose-6-phosphatase**, so its glucose-6-phosphate cannot leave the cell as free glucose
whyNot.B: Heart is also **muscle without glucose-6-phosphatase**; it keeps its glycogen for its own use
whyNot.D: A **small store**; the kidney adds glucose mainly by **gluconeogenesis in prolonged fasting**, not after one night
whyNot.E: A **tiny store**, used by the brain itself; it does not export glucose to blood

why: The **liver** has **glucose-6-phosphatase**, so glycogen breakdown ends in **free glucose** that enters the blood. Muscle lacks this enzyme, so its glycogen is used **inside the muscle** only.

idea.rule: Only organs with glucose-6-phosphatase can put glucose into the blood.
also: Liver: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Kidney cortex: gluconeogenesis in prolonged fasting
Muscle: lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen fuels only muscle
Von Gierke disease: absent enzyme gives fasting hypoglycemia

stem: Hepatocytes from a fasted animal are incubated with labeled pyruvate while they make glucose. The first labeled product is a four-carbon compound made by a biotin- and ATP-dependent carboxylase that acetyl-CoA activates. This product cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane and is first reduced to malate to reach the enzyme that makes phosphoenolpyruvate.
oneliner: Fasting hepatocytes + labeled pyruvate → 4-carbon product by biotin carboxylase + must leave as malate → made where?
ask: In which compartment is the first labeled product formed?

whyNot.B: Holds **PEP carboxykinase**; the product must travel as malate to reach it, so it is made elsewhere
whyNot.C: Lies **outside the inner membrane**, but the product cannot cross that membrane, so it is made inside it
whyNot.D: Holds **glucose-6-phosphatase**, the last step of the pathway, not the first
whyNot.E: Shortens **very-long-chain fatty acids**; it has no pyruvate carboxylase

why: **Pyruvate carboxylase** (biotin, ATP, activated by acetyl-CoA) makes **oxaloacetate** in the **mitochondrial matrix**. With no inner-membrane carrier for it, oxaloacetate leaves as **malate** (or aspartate) and is rebuilt in the cytosol for PEP carboxykinase.

idea.rule: Gluconeogenesis starts in the mitochondrion, runs in the cytosol and ends in the ER.
also: Pyruvate carboxylase: mitochondrial, needs biotin and ATP
PEP carboxykinase: cytosolic, makes PEP from oxaloacetate
Oxaloacetate leaves the matrix as malate or aspartate
Glucose-6-phosphatase: ER lumen, last step

stem: A 4-month-old boy is floppy and feeds poorly. He has a large tongue and a markedly enlarged heart with a short PR interval. Blood glucose is normal. A muscle biopsy shows vacuoles filled with glycogen.
oneliner: 4-mo M + hypotonia + macroglossia + huge heart + short PR + normal glucose + glycogen vacuoles → where is glycogen stored?
ask: Glycogen is accumulating within which cellular compartment?

whyNot.A: Normal glycogen granules lie free here; **cytosolic** storage fits debranching or phosphorylase defects, not these **membrane-bound vacuoles**
whyNot.B: Not a glycogen site; mitochondrial disease gives **lactic acidosis** and ragged-red fibers
whyNot.C: Accumulates **very-long-chain fatty acids** in Zellweger disease, not glycogen
whyNot.D: Holds **glucose-6-phosphatase** in liver, but defects there give fasting hypoglycemia, which he lacks

why: **Acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase)** works in the **lysosome**, so its loss fills lysosomes with glycogen. The heart and muscle swell, and **blood glucose stays normal** because liver glycogenolysis is intact.

idea.rule: Pompe disease is the glycogen storage disease that is also a lysosomal storage disease.
also: Pompe: cardiomegaly, hypotonia, early death without enzyme replacement
Tay-Sachs: GM2 ganglioside in lysosomes
Gaucher: glucocerebroside in lysosomes
Niemann-Pick: sphingomyelin in lysosomes

stem: Hepatocytes are taken from an animal fed a high-carbohydrate meal and begin making palmitate from acetyl-CoA. Citrate carries the acetyl units out of the mitochondrion, acetyl-CoA carboxylase is active, and the pathway consumes NADPH.
oneliner: Hepatocytes after a high-carbohydrate meal + citrate exports acetyl-CoA + NADPH needed → palmitate made where?
ask: In which compartment does fatty acid synthase make palmitate?

whyNot.A: Site of **beta-oxidation**, the opposite pathway, which is switched off by malonyl-CoA
whyNot.B: Shortens **very-long-chain fatty acids**; it does not build palmitate from acetyl-CoA
whyNot.C: Elongates and desaturates **after palmitate exists**; it is not the first synthesis step
whyNot.E: Holds DNA and transcription machinery; no lipid synthesis from acetyl-CoA here

why: Citrate leaves the matrix and is cleaved to acetyl-CoA, so **acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase** work in the **cytosol**, using NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway. Beta-oxidation is **mitochondrial**.

idea.rule: Fatty acid synthesis is cytosolic; fatty acid breakdown is mitochondrial.
also: Citrate shuttle exports acetyl-CoA
NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme
Malonyl-CoA inhibits carnitine acyltransferase I
Beta-oxidation: mitochondrial matrix

stem: In a cell culture experiment, a drug that selectively blocks RNA polymerase I stops the production of one class of RNA, the most abundant RNA in the cell. Its large 45S precursor is cut into smaller products that join proteins to form the subunits of the translation machinery.
oneliner: Pol I blocked → loss of 45S precursor and ribosomal subunit assembly → site of this RNA's synthesis?
ask: Where in the cell is this RNA class transcribed?

whyNot.A: Where **Pol II and Pol III** make mRNA and tRNA, not the 45S precursor
whyNot.C: Has its own polymerase for **mtDNA** genes; it makes no 45S precursor
whyNot.D: Holds **mature ribosomes** in action, but has no DNA template for this RNA
whyNot.E: A **protein meshwork** under the inner nuclear membrane; it is not a transcription site

answer: Nucleolus (rRNA transcribed by RNA polymerase I)
why: **RNA polymerase I** transcribes the **45S pre-rRNA** in the **nucleolus**, where subunits are also assembled. It is processed to 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNA; 5S rRNA comes from polymerase III elsewhere.

idea.rule: Pol I: nucleolus, rRNA; Pol II: mRNA; Pol III: tRNA.
also: Pol II: mRNA, snRNA, miRNA; blocked by alpha-amanitin
Pol III: tRNA and 5S rRNA
Nucleolus is the site of ribosomal subunit assembly
Nucleoli are prominent in rapidly dividing cells

stem: A researcher compares one gene's RNA in two tissues. A long precursor transcript is found in the nucleus and a shorter version in the cytoplasm. The two tissues make different protein isoforms from this same gene, and removal of the missing segments depends on small nuclear ribonucleoproteins.
oneliner: Nuclear precursor → shorter cytoplasmic mRNA + tissue isoforms + snRNPs → where are introns removed?
ask: Where does removal of these segments take place?

whyNot.A: Ribosomes **translate** finished mRNA; they do not remove introns
whyNot.B: Handles **translation of secretory proteins** and folding, not RNA processing
whyNot.C: Modifies and **sorts proteins**; it contains no spliceosome
whyNot.D: Have their own **small genome without introns** in human cells; not the site for nuclear gene splicing

why: The **spliceosome**, built from **snRNPs**, cuts out **introns** from pre-mRNA in the **nucleus** before export. Alternative splicing explains different **isoforms** from one gene.

idea.rule: Splicing is nuclear and co-transcriptional; translation is cytoplasmic.
also: Anti-Smith antibodies target snRNPs in SLE
Alternative splicing gives tissue-specific isoforms
5' cap and poly-A tail are also added in the nucleus
Beta-thalassemia can arise from splice-site mutations

stem: A protein is lost from the nuclei of cultured cells, which then show a misshapen, fragile nuclear envelope. The protein is an intermediate filament that lies just under the inner nuclear membrane and is phosphorylated at the start of mitosis to help break down the envelope.
oneliner: Intermediate filament under inner nuclear membrane + phosphorylated in mitosis + lost → fragile misshapen nuclei → where does it belong?
ask: Which structure normally contains this protein?

whyNot.B: Contains **laminin**, a different, sound-alike glycoprotein that is not an intermediate filament
whyNot.C: Built from **nucleoporins** that pass material through the envelope, not intermediate filaments
whyNot.D: Organizes **microtubules** from centrioles; not made of lamins
whyNot.E: A site of **rRNA synthesis** with no envelope-supporting meshwork

why: **Lamins** are intermediate filaments forming the **nuclear lamina** under the inner nuclear membrane, giving shape. Mitotic **phosphorylation** disassembles it; laminin is a **basement membrane** protein.

idea.rule: Lamin lines the nucleus; laminin lines the basement membrane.
also: Progeria: lamin A mutation
Vimentin: intermediate filament of mesenchymal cells
Keratin: intermediate filament of epithelia
Desmin: intermediate filament of muscle

stem: Chromatin is exposed to mild nuclease digestion. Gel electrophoresis of the DNA shows a regular ladder of fragments, with the core particles protecting about 146 base pairs each. The bound proteins are rich in positively charged lysine and arginine, and the chromatin looks like beads on a string.
oneliner: Mild nuclease + ladder of DNA fragments + 146 bp core + beads on a string → which histone binds the spacer DNA?
ask: Which histone binds the DNA between the beads?

whyNot.A: Part of the **core octamer** around which DNA is wound, not the linker
whyNot.B: Also in the **core octamer** with H2A, protected from nuclease
whyNot.D: Core octamer member; its **tail** is the site of many methylation marks
whyNot.E: Core octamer member, forms a **tetramer with H3**, and is inside the 146 bp particle

why: The nucleosome core is DNA wound around an **octamer of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4**. **Histone H1** binds the **linker DNA** between nucleosomes and helps compact chromatin; nuclease cuts the linker first.

idea.rule: Core histones are inside the bead; H1 holds the string between beads.
also: Histones are rich in lysine and arginine
Acetylation loosens chromatin for transcription
Deacetylation and methylation silence chromatin
Heterochromatin is more tightly packed than euchromatin
